title: Review: The Gen 6 Santa Cruz Tallboy is VPP-Free and Thriving
content:
Earlier this year, Santa Cruz completely overhauled the Tallboy, its popular short-travel trail bike. The redesign included a slightly slacker head tube angle, a lighter frame, and the addition of 10mm of travel at both ends. The biggest story, however, was the move away from Santa Cruz’s longstanding VPP suspension platform to a simpler 4-bar Horst-Link layout. This last design change led many to question why they would even buy a Santa Cruz without its brand-defining suspension platform.

When the Gen 6 Tallboy was announced, I was immediately interested in testing it. As someone who enjoys short- to mid-travel trail bikes, I got along pretty well with the past two generations of the Tallboy — they were nearly identical, after all. That said, I felt the previous Tallboys had some limitations, and the VPP suspension platform has never really been my favorite, which is why the Gen 6 redesign appealed to me so much.  

I got my hands on the latest Tallboy back in August and have been riding it off and on until just recently. I’ve pedaled it for hundreds of miles on the trails in and around Reno, NV, and the greater Lake Tahoe area. I can confidently say that the Tallboy is more capable and versatile than its predecessors, and is easily the best version yet. It’s a freaking blast to ride, and I sure wish I didn’t have to send it back.

What’s New?

We covered the Gen 6 updates to the Tallboy in our launch article several months back. You can check that out here if you want to revisit the details. Long story short, there were some major changes, most notably bumping travel to 130mm in the rear and 140mm up front, and the move to the aforementioned 4-bar Horst link suspension layout. With 120mm XC bikes, including the new Santa Cruz Blur, growing increasingly capable, the overlap in the lineup and the weight penalty of the previous Tallboy wasn’t making much sense anymore, and the increase in travel moves the Gen 6 more squarely into trail bike territory.

Of course, the move away from VPP means the frame’s silhouette has also changed a little bit with a less complex linkage and pivots on the chainstays. This also allowed for a straighter seat tube with increased insertion, making it easier to run longer travel droppers. Santa Cruz wisely carried over its well-executed in-frame storage, normal internal cable routing, threaded bottom bracket, and molded rubber protection on the downtube, bottom bracket, and chainstay. It has all the features we’ve grown accustomed to on modern mountain bikes.

The Gen 6 Tallboy frame is offered in Santa Cruz’s top-tier CC carbon fiber only, and it’s still a dedicated 29” bike, no mullet option here. While its travel has increased, Santa Cruz claims it reduced frame weight by ~300 grams. Geometry-wise, Santa Cruz made some tweaks but didn’t deviate too far from the existing formula. The biggest change is a slightly slacker head tube angle, at 65.1° in high and 64.8° in the low flip-chip setting. Adjusting the flip chip also changes the bottom bracket height by +/-3mm. 

First Impressions 

Right out of the box, the Tallboy started making a strong impression. I’d argue that the updated frame and 4-bar layout have a clean, modern look, and the Gen 6 is the best-looking version yet. The dark purple frame with reflective silver logos really did it for me, and proved to be attention-grabbing out on the trail, too. At just over 29 pounds in the XO AXS RSV build, it’s also respectably lightweight for a 130/140mm trail bike. On the first ride, the low weight was immediately apparent in its snappy handling and willingness to get up and go.

A Questionable Front Tire Spec 

The stock Maxxis Forekaster tire spec undoubtedly contributed to its spirited, fast-rolling nature, and this bike simply felt quick, responsive, and efficient up, down, and all around. Those tires are not only quick, but they’re surprisingly grippy in the right conditions, too. Grippy enough that they lulled me into a false sense of trust and confidence. I think the Forekaster is an excellent rear tire, but it quickly became apparent it was not the ideal front tire in the typically loose and loose-over-hard conditions in my area. 

I ran the stock tire setup for the first couple of weeks, but after washing out the front tire numerous times — one of which resulted in a very hard crash — I swapped the front tire out for a more aggressive Kenda Double Diamond Trail. I eventually swapped the rear tire out for the new Kenda Ripper Trail, and ran that setup for the remainder of my testing. This simple tire swap made an enormous difference in the Tallboy’s performance, and highlighted the importance of matching your tires to both your conditions and riding style. 

This tire swap took the Tallboy from fast, fun, and kinda squirrelly to fast, fun, and way more predictable. Being able to trust the grip of the front tire significantly boosted my confidence and allowed me to ride the Tallboy way harder. Of course, the dual Forekaster setup may be ideal for some riders and locations, but if I could do it again, I’d switch out the front tire for something more aggressive before the first ride, and I’d probably recommend that most riders do the same — unless you primarily ride mellower terrain and/or hero dirt.

Climbing

Right out of the gate, one of the first things I noticed about the Tallboy was its more relaxed seated pedaling position. The 475mm reach and 76.5° effective seat tube angle are almost exactly the same as the previous version, but the stack is a bit taller, and there’s no shortage of adjustability in the front end.

The XO build I was testing came with a 35mm rise OneUp Carbon V2 handlebar, Race Face Turbine SL stem (flippable for +/-6mm rise), and 40mm of stack height to play with. I tinkered around a bit, but landed roughly in the middle of the available adjustment range. The point being, it’s got a fairly trail-oriented pedaling position that I found to be quite comfortable for a bike with its (bordering on XC-bike-esque) climbing performance and efficiency. 

I always thought the pedaling performance of VPP was one of its best attributes, but it sacrificed sensitivity and generally felt a bit harsher for it. In my opinion, the Gen 6 Tallboy’s 4-bar suspension offers significantly more comfort over small bumps and trail chatter, great climbing traction, and it doesn’t sacrifice much, if any, pedaling support or efficiency — even with 10mm more travel. That’s hard to quantify, of course, but I was genuinely surprised to see my climb times on Strava pretty much neck and neck with the Pivot Mach 4 SL I was riding for much of the summer. 

Still, it’s not an XC bike, nor is it pretending to be. But I think Santa Cruz did an excellent job with the suspension to improve rider comfort while still delivering the efficient pedaling performance expected from a lighter trail bike. It was similar to the Allied FITZ in that I felt I could ride faster, farther, and for longer, while staying fresher than on some other bikes in the same travel bracket. 

I found its handling to be sharp, and it was easy to maneuver in tight spaces and technical sections of trail, and I was genuinely surprised by just how zippy and energetic it felt on single track, fire roads, even on the pavement. I had no issues navigating tight switchbacks and always found ample traction at the rear wheel when scrambling over rocks, steps, or loose, blown-out surfaces. That said, the bottom bracket is fairly low at sag, and I definitely encountered a few rock strikes when pedaling through techy spots. It’s 3mm higher in the high flip chip setting, but again, still relatively low.

Descending

Both of the previous Tallboy generations were very adept and capable on the descents, particularly in their short travel context. If you ever rode either of those bikes, then you’re probably aware their only real limitations were their suspension travel and what you were willing to ride them down. Not surprisingly, the Gen 6’s 4-bar suspension, increased travel, and slacker head tube angle all combine to enhance its downhill capability compared to the previous version. At the same time, the Tallboy doesn’t lose the lively, nimble, and downright playful character that helps define its downhill performance.

It’s easy enough to throw around the words “ more capable”, but what exactly does that mean? In the case of the Tallboy, it is undoubtedly a better descender than its predecessor for several reasons. First, and perhaps most obviously, it has more travel to soak up bigger hits, get you out of trouble, or, in my case, help offset my general lack of descending skill. I know 10mm may not sound like a lot, but it makes an outsized difference on a shorter travel bike like the Tallboy. At the same time, it doesn’t really add any weight or try to turn it into something it’s not.

Second, I believe the 4-bar platform provides a more well-rounded suspension performance. While I appreciated the mid-stroke support and big-hit performance of VPP, I always felt it lacked sensitivity off the top, and it transmitted a fair amount of feedback to the rider. With the 4-bar layout and revised kinematics on the Gen 6, Santa Cruz delivers a much better balance throughout the travel.

It’s more supple and responsive right off the top, mid-stroke is still supportive and poppy when you want it to be, and there’s enough progression at the end of travel to avoid bottom-outs unless you’re doing something stupid. Don’t get me wrong, the VPP Tallboy was good, but I think the 4-bar Tallboy is much better.

Third, the refreshed geometry brings it up to date without taking it too far. The head tube angle is marginally slacker, which undoubtedly helps enhance stability at speed and composure in steep terrain. The higher stack also contributes to a more confident descending position. Still, these are fairly subtle changes that don’t detract from its responsive handling feel, at least in my experience. Personally, I’m glad they didn’t make it much slacker or try to turn the Tallboy into some kind of wannabe mini-enduro bike, because I think it’s just right the way it is.

Overall, the Gen 6 Tallboy is smoother, calmer, and more confidence-inspiring on the descents than its predecessors. It’s far from a plow-machine, and it still rewards good line choices, but the margin for error is a bit greater. And thankfully, the Gen 6 update didn’t rob it of its spunky and playful attitude. I found myself pulling up to manual through all the dips and popping off just about every roll and side hit on the trail, no matter how small. It might not have inspired me to ride everything as fast as possible, but it certainly had me squeezing all the fun I could out of every ride.

The Build

The XO AXS RSV build I tested is second from the top of the line, and comes in under the $10K mark. As expected, it’s pretty much perfect right out of the box, and there are almost zero component changes I’d make out of the box. Hell, Santa Cruz even spec’d the AXS Rocker paddle shifter, so I don’t even have the AXS Pod ergonomics to complain about. The RockShox Ultimate level suspension and Reserve 30 SL wheels are top-notch and help contribute to the smooth and damp ride quality. The SRAM Motive 4-piston brakes paired with thicker HS2 rotors offered ample stopping power. My old wrists also appreciated the OneUp Carbon V2 handlebar. 

Other than the front tire spec, which is down to personal preference and easily changed, I only found one other thing to complain about, and that’s the OneUp V3 dropper. I’m a huge fan of OneUp’s affordable droppers, and I have been for years. Two of the three V3 droppers I’ve ridden this year have worked flawlessly. I couldn’t figure out what was going on with this one, but it made a subtle but pretty annoying knocking noise when descending over rough, chattery terrain. It was particularly notable given how silent the bike was otherwise. 

My Takeaway

Santa Cruz made the bold and somewhat divisive choice to ditch its VPP suspension design in favor of the simpler 4-bar layout, and I think the Tallboy is a better bike for it. In my opinion, it provides a more balanced, well-rounded suspension performance without detracting from its efficiency or muting its playful character. The bump in suspension travel and refined geometry are also welcome additions that enhance its composure and capability and position it more squarely as the true do-it-all trail bike it is. 

These days, there are lots of amazing mountain bikes on the market, and the Gen 6 Tallboy is one of the best I’ve ridden all year. Unless you’re riding aggressive enduro-style terrain all the time, this is a bike you can jump on for pretty much any ride and have a great time. Most importantly, it’s a heck of a lot of fun to ride, and that’s the whole point.
